messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Luca is a 25-year-old salesman who came to treatment after months of feeling as if his body still lived in a war zone even though he had long since returned to the United States. During a period abroad as a civilian, he was caught in repeated shelling in a dense urban area. He described nights as the worst: the thin walls of the apartment where he had been staying seemed to vibrate before each blast, and darkness made everything harder to track. He remembered sitting fully dressed on the floor with other civilians, straining to hear whether the next sound was distant or close, whether footsteps in the stairwell meant someone fleeing or something worse. What stayed with him most was not a single image but the sustained sense that danger could arrive without warning, especially after dark, when every sound seemed amplified and unknowable.

Since coming home, Luca has continued to live with intense fear, bursts of horror, and a persistent current of anger that he finds hard to explain to people around him. He also carries guilt and shame about having survived and left when others did not, though he struggles to put this into words. He says that by evening his whole body changes; as daylight fades, he becomes keyed up and watchful, certain that nighttime is when things become unsafe. He checks locks repeatedly and listens for sounds outside his apartment with the same strained attention he once used overseas. His girlfriend has noticed that he becomes tense and irritable after sunset and is much more able to relax, if at all, in the morning or early afternoon.

The problem shows up in his work in concrete ways. As a salesperson, he spends his day moving between a showroom floor, phone calls, and customer conversations that require him to stay engaged and persuasive. Lately he has found it difficult to concentrate even during routine interactions. A customer will be explaining what they want and Luca realizes he has lost track of the details, his mind snagged on some vague sense that something is wrong or about to happen. If he is working a late shift and the store is quieter, the unease becomes more obvious; normal evening noises in the building pull his attention away, and he catches himself scanning rather than listening. He has begun making small mistakes with orders and forgetting parts of conversations, which is troubling for someone who used to take pride in being quick and personable.

At home, the nights remain the clearest marker of how much his world has narrowed. He does not describe elaborate rituals or a long list of symptoms; instead, he talks about an atmosphere of danger that settles over him as soon as it gets dark. He feels fear first, then anger at himself for reacting this way, then shame when he sees how much effort it takes just to sit through an ordinary evening. He often stays mentally on guard deep into the night, listening, checking, trying to feel sure that the apartment is secure. Because sleep comes only after hours of vigilance, the next day he is mentally foggy, and concentrating on sales numbers, customer preferences, or even simple administrative tasks feels more difficult than it used to.

Luca is in a relationship and says his girlfriend has tried to be patient, but he can tell she does not fully understand why nighttime affects him so strongly. He worries about seeming weak or damaged, especially because outwardly he is back at work, functioning, and young enough that other people assume he should have “moved on.” What finally brought him in was a recent evening at work when he lost focus during a straightforward sales conversation and felt a sudden surge of fear so strong that he had to step into the back room to collect himself. That incident frightened him not because anything happened, but because it made him realize how little control he feels he has once night approaches. He is seeking help now because he wants to be able to come home after dark without bracing for danger, to focus at work again, and to stop feeling that every evening pulls him back toward something he survived but has not really left.
